findings.issue_text: pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go:123 — [P1, confidence 100] The negative-miss shape creates reference×credential fan-out because `cachedPerms, err := s.getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)` followed by `if allowed { ... return ... }` and the fall-through `permissions, err := s.getIdentityPermissions(...)` requery the same complete user/action permission set for every distinct unauthorized `(name,parent)`, so sequential checks over N unseen resources issue N identical permission-store queries and materialize N cardinality-unbounded denial entries; trigger: one cached permission snapshot plus many unique inaccessible resource names; strongest author counterargument: per-resource denials preserve the chance that a cached miss is a newly granted permission; rebuttal: refreshing the whole snapshot on the first miss does not make later absent names less authoritative, so freshness is represented twice without a version; wrong-shape/simplification advisory: make the permission snapshot carry freshness/version and delete `permDenialCache`, `userPermDenialCacheKey`, and the second boolean cache wrapper.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go:30 — [P1, confidence 100] The denial key omits the identity discriminator in `return namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent`, so a denial cached for `anonymous:0` on a dashboard is returned for the supported `render:0` identity checking the same tuple even though `getRendererPermissions` grants that action; trigger: anonymous and renderer requests in the same namespace using their built-in UID `0`; failure mode: one identity's derived state denies a different identity before type-specific dispatch; strongest author counterargument: UIDs uniquely identify principals; rebuttal: this code and its surrounding tests explicitly model both anonymous and renderer identities with UID `0`; wrong-shape advisory: include `IdentityType` in a structured, collision-safe key.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go:31 — [P2, confidence 100] The delimiter-concatenated key `namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent` is non-injective, so `(name="a_b", parent="c")` and `(name="a", parent="b_c")` produce the same entry and a denial for the first resource poisons the second; trigger: two valid request strings containing underscores at different field boundaries; failure mode: cached decisions bleed across unrelated resource/folder associations; strongest author counterargument: identifier validation prevents delimiter characters; rebuttal: this service does not validate either field and its surrounding checks already use underscore-bearing names such as `some_dashboard`; wrong-shape advisory: length-prefix or hash typed fields as the authlib client does instead of encoding a tuple with magic separators.

pkg/services/authz/rbac.go:101 — [P2, confidence 100] Cache ownership is coupled to deployment topology because the in-process constructor installs `authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{})` while `newRemoteRBACClient` at line 162 installs a 30-second local cache, so repeated allowed checks in the default mode traverse validation, service cache decoding, permission evaluation, and folder inheritance every time while the identical cloud/standalone workload short-circuits at the client; trigger: a hot allowed resource checked repeatedly; failure mode: this change regresses default-mode CPU work and gives the same API mode-dependent cache/load semantics; strongest author counterargument: an in-process channel is cheap and the server permission cache still avoids SQL; rebuttal: the removed exact-result cache bypassed the entire service path, including folder-tree work, and none of those costs disappear merely because transport is local; coupling/simplification advisory: choose one cache owner across all constructors—if the service owns it, delete the remote `cache.NewLocalCache(...)` layer too, or if clients own it, delete the new server denial-cache layer.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go:31 — [P1 blocker, confidence 100] Verbatim `return namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent` omits the identity type, so after the supported `anonymous:0` identity is denied `dashboards:read` for `dash1`, the supported `render:0` identity checking the same tuple hits the identical denial key and returns false at `service.go:117-120` instead of receiving the renderer wildcard grant.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go:31 — [P2 blocker, confidence 100] Verbatim `return namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent` concatenates unescaped resource identifiers, so a denial for `(name="dash_a", parent="b")` and a later allowed check for `(name="dash", parent="a_b")` produce the same key and the latter is falsely denied.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go:982 — [P2 blocker, confidence 100] Verbatim `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}` makes the explicit-denial-cache test pass even when the early denial-cache return is removed or broken because the cached permission cannot allow and the empty fallback store also denies, leaving the core negative-cache short-circuit acceptance criterion unverified.

pkg/services/authz/rbac.go:101 — [P3 advisory, confidence 100] Verbatim `rbacClient := authzlib.NewClient(` duplicates client construction across the in-process and remote paths, so any future shared option added to only one constructor makes authorization behavior mode-dependent; the strongest counterargument is that the two modes intentionally require different cache policies, but that does not justify duplicating tracer and future common options because a helper accepting the cache policy would preserve that distinction and make the duplicated construction unnecessary.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go:131 — P1, confidence 100: verbatim `if allowed { ... return &authzv1.CheckResponse{Allowed: allowed}, nil }`; when an administrator revokes a permission while its grant remains in `permCache`, this early return runs before the database fetch at line 139 and continues authorizing the revoked access until the cache entry expires.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go:123 — P2 (confidence 100): `cachedPerms, err := s.getCachedIdentityPermissions(ctx, checkReq.Namespace, checkReq.IdentityType, checkReq.UserUID, checkReq.Action)` followed by `if err == nil {` treats every identifier-store error as a cache miss and line 139 immediately calls `getIdentityPermissions` (whose user path calls `GetUserIdentifiers` again), so works today, breaks when the identifier cache is cold during database degradation because every Check/List request performs the failing lookup twice, doubling backend pressure and latency before returning the same error; the strongest author counterargument is that an immediate retry can recover a transient failure, but it fails because there is no backoff, in-flight deduplication, or miss/error classification and persistent failures are amplified across every concurrent authorization request.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go:116 — P2 (confidence 100): `permDenialKey := userPermDenialCacheKey(checkReq.Namespace.Value, checkReq.UserUID, checkReq.Action, checkReq.Name, checkReq.ParentFolder)` keys denials by the caller-provided identifier while line 360 keys permissions by resolved `userIdentifiers.UID`, so works today, breaks when the same identity is addressed sometimes by numeric ID and sometimes by UID because the two denial entries independently miss and force redundant permission-store refreshes with inconsistent cache-hit behavior; the strongest author counterargument is that clients should always send canonical UIDs, but it fails because `GetUserIdentifiers` explicitly accepts numeric IDs via `strconv.Atoi(userUID)`, making both representations supported inputs.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go:31 — [P2, confidence 100] Verbatim `return namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent` omits the identity type, so an anonymous request that produces a denial for supported subject `anonymous:0` and a dashboard tuple stores exactly the key later used by supported subject `render:0`, whose check then exits at `service.go:117-120` before its hardcoded renderer grant and disables rendering for that dashboard; although the cache stores only denials for 30 seconds, repeating the anonymous request after each expiry sustains the cross-principal availability attack indefinitely.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go:982 — P1 / confidence 100 / spec-coverage advisory: the denial-cache test's supposed contrary grant is verbatim `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`, so deleting both denial-cache read and write behavior from `Check` leaves this test green through the ordinary cached/database deny path; trigger/consequence: a regression that stops negative caching is released undetected and every denied request returns to the database; strongest author counterargument: the manual `s.permDenialCache.Set(..., true)` isolates the read fast path, but that fails because the fallback is also configured to deny and the production write lifecycle is never exercised.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go:829 — P1 / confidence 100 / fragile-structure advisory: every anonymous and renderer case starts with verbatim `s := setupService()` (again at line 878), preventing the suite from exercising the shared cache across identity types; trigger/consequence: after `anonymous:0` is denied `dashboards:read` on `dash1`, a subsequent `render:0` check for that dashboard on the same `Service` is incorrectly denied by the colliding denial key while all tests remain green; strongest author counterargument: fresh services provide proper subtest isolation, but that fails because cross-request cache state is the production behavior these tests must verify.

pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go:919 — P2 / confidence 100: the warm-cache test ends with only verbatim `require.NoError(t, err)` and `assert.True(t, resp.Allowed)` (and `TestService_CacheList` likewise asserts only output), so a regression that still queries the store on every cache hit remains green and defeats the change's database-load reduction; strongest author counterargument: cache-only fixture data proves the cached value contributes to the response, but that fails because the permissive `fakeStore` records calls without failing and neither cache-hit test asserts those call counts are zero.

pkg/services/authz/rbac.go:103 — P2 / confidence 100 / spec-coverage advisory: the deployment-mode split expressed by verbatim `authzlib.WithCacheClientOption(&NoopCache{})` has no request-level test through `ProvideAuthZClient` or `newRemoteRBACClient`, so swapping or dropping the in-process no-op versus remote local-cache wiring remains green and causes the in-process path to regain a second stale decision cache or the remote path to lose its cache; strongest author counterargument: the option calls are direct and `NoopCache` is trivial, but that fails because both cache implementations satisfy the same interface and the changed service tests construct `Service` directly, never observing client-layer wiring.

goldens.comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.
The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/authz/rbac/service.go:123 — [P1, confidence 100] The negative-miss shape creates reference×credential fan-out because `cachedPerms, err := s.getCachedIdentityPermissions(...)` followed by `if allowed { ... return ... }` and the fall-through `permissions, err := s.getIdentityPermissions(...)` requery the same complete user/action permission set for every distinct unauthorized `(name,parent)`, so sequential checks over N unseen resources issue N identical permission-store queries and materialize N cardinality-unbounded denial entries; trigger: one cached permission snapshot plus many unique inaccessible resource names; strongest author counterargument: per-resource denials preserve the chance that a cached miss is a newly granted permission; rebuttal: refreshing the whole snapshot on the first miss does not make later absent names less authoritative, so freshness is represented twice without a version; wrong-shape/simplification advisory: make the permission snapshot carry freshness/version and delete `permDenialCache`, `userPermDenialCacheKey`, and the second boolean cache wrapper.

adjudication.rationale: The finding identifies a real architectural concern in the diff. Looking at the code flow in service.go lines 113-150: (1) check permDenialCache, (2) check cached permissions via getCachedIdentityPermissions, (3) if cache miss or not allowed, call getIdentityPermissions to fetch from DB, (4) if denied, store in permDenialCache. The concern is valid: for N distinct unauthorized (name, parent) combinations, the code will: first check denial cache (miss), then check permission cache (may hit but resource not in allowed set), then fall through to getIdentityPermissions (full DB query), then cache the denial. This creates N denial cache entries and potentially N DB queries for the same user/action permission set. However, this is more of an architectural/efficiency concern than a bug - the code is functionally correct. The finding's suggestion to use versioned permission snapshots instead of per-resource denial caching is a valid design critique but represents a scope/architecture concern rather than a defect.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real architectural inconsistency introduced by this diff. The in-process path (line 101) now uses NoopCache{} which disables client-side caching, while the remote path (line 162) uses cache.NewLocalCache with 30-second expiry. This creates mode-dependent caching behavior. However, this is not a 'bug' per se - the code will function correctly. The diff shows the server-side now has its own caching layer (permDenialCache, permCache) that handles caching at the service level. adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go:31 — [P1 blocker, confidence 100] Verbatim `return namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent` omits the identity type, so after the supported `anonymous:0` identity is denied `dashboards:read` for `dash1`, the supported `render:0` identity checking the same tuple hits the identical denial key and returns false at `service.go:117-120` instead of receiving the renderer wildcard grant.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that anonymous and render identities would share the same denial cache key, causing cross-contamination. However, examining the code flow: (1) The denial cache key includes userUID which differs between identity types - anonymous would have a different userUID than render service. (2) Looking at service.go, the Check function extracts checkReq.UserUID from the request subject, which would be different for different identity types. (3) The finding assumes 'anonymous:0' and 'render:0' would produce identical cache keys, but the userUID component ('0' vs '0') would only be the same if both identities happen to have the same UID portion, which is a specific edge case not demonstrated by the diff. (4) More importantly, the render service path in getCachedIdentityPermissions returns cache.ErrNotFound immediately (line 347-348), so it wouldn't even use the permission denial cache lookup. The finding misreads how the identity type affects the cache key through the userUID parameter.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go:31 — [P2 blocker, confidence 100] Verbatim `return namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent` concatenates unescaped resource identifiers, so a denial for `(name="dash_a", parent="b")` and a later allowed check for `(name="dash", parent="a_b")` produce the same key and the latter is falsely denied.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a key collision vulnerability in the cache key generation. Looking at line 31 in cache.go, the function `userPermDenialCacheKey` concatenates `namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent` without any escaping. This means that different combinations of name and parent values containing underscores could produce identical cache keys. For example, (name="dash_a", parent="b") and (name="dash", parent="a_b") would both produce the same key suffix "_dash_a_b". This is a real bug that could cause false denials when the denial cache is checked in service.go lines 115-119.

The code in `store.go` (referenced by the finding) does accept numeric IDs via `strconv.Atoi(userUID)`, meaning the same user could be addressed by different identifiers. adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/authz/rbac/cache.go:31 — [P2, confidence 100] Verbatim `return namespace + ".perm_" + userUID + "_" + action + "_" + name + "_" + parent` omits the identity type, so an anonymous request that produces a denial for supported subject `anonymous:0` and a dashboard tuple stores exactly the key later used by supported subject `render:0`, whose check then exits at `service.go:117-120` before its hardcoded renderer grant and disables rendering for that dashboard; although the cache stores only denials for 30 seconds, repeating the anonymous request after each expiry sustains the cross-principal availability attack indefinitely.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that anonymous requests and render service requests would share the same cache key, but examining the code flow shows this is incorrect. In service.go, the getCachedIdentityPermissions function (lines 339-373) handles TypeAnonymous and TypeRenderService differently - TypeRenderService returns cache.ErrNotFound immediately (line 351), meaning it never checks the permDenialCache. The permDenialCache check at lines 117-120 happens before getCachedIdentityPermissions is called, but the cache key includes the userUID which would be different for anonymous vs render service (anonymous:0 vs render:0 based on the subject parsing). The identity type is embedded in the userUID parameter passed to userPermDenialCacheKey, not as a separate field. The finding misreads how the cache keys are constructed and how different identity types flow through the code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/authz/rbac/service_test.go:982 — P1 / confidence 100 / spec-coverage advisory: the denial-cache test's supposed contrary grant is verbatim `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}`, so deleting both denial-cache read and write behavior from `Check` leaves this test green through the ordinary cached/database deny path; trigger/consequence: a regression that stops negative caching is released undetected and every denied request returns to the database; strongest author counterargument: the manual `s.permDenialCache.Set(..., true)` isolates the read fast path, but that fails because the fallback is also configured to deny and the production write lifecycle is never exercised.

adjudication.rationale: The finding raises a valid test coverage concern. Looking at the test 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry' (lines 970-991), it sets up a denial cache entry and a permCache entry with `false` value. The test verifies denial is returned, but as the finding notes, if the denial cache check were removed, the test would still pass because: 1) the permCache lookup would succeed, 2) checkPermission would be called with a map containing `dash1: false`, which would deny access anyway. The test doesn't properly isolate the denial cache behavior - it should set up conditions where the permCache would ALLOW access (e.g., `dash1: true`) to prove the denial cache takes precedence. This is a legitimate test quality concern for newly added caching logic, though the severity is debatable since the denial cache is an optimization, not a correctness feature.
